source.title: Does Transliteration Help Multilingual Language Modeling?
source.authors: Ibraheem Muhammad Moosa; Mahmud Elahi Akhter; Ashfia Binte Habib

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-lingual representation similarity in multilingual language models under a transliteration setting, but does not test the claim's scale trend or its specified cross-modal, seed, mapping, feature, or metric-dependence versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream-task performance, tokenizer statistics, and CKA results. Only the CKA results bear on representation similarity; downstream performance and tokenizer results are not rows for this claim. CKA values are shown only in Figure 1, without numerical values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study measures within-model cross-lingual CKA between parallel sentences in different languages, comparing transliterated and original-script pretraining. It does not compare independently trained models, seeds, modalities, mappings or features on the same inputs. It also has no scale trend. So its results do not bear on whether representations of different models converge. It neither tests nor relies on the convergence claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that transliteration significantly improves downstream performance for low-resource Indic languages without hurting high-resource ones (Mann-Whitney U tests). The higher, more stable cross-lingual CKA of uni-script models is offered as an explanation, read as better cross-lingual representations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CKA, but measures layerwise similarity across language versions of parallel sentences in multilingual models; it does not test alignment growth with model scale or compare independently trained models on identical inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: The layerwise pattern differs: the authors report that multi-script CLRS is low from layer nine, while uni-script CLRS remains high until layer eleven; all models' CLRS drops significantly at the last layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Uni-script (transliterated) models keep high cross-lingual CKA until layer 11, while multi-script models are low from layer 9. CKA drops at the last layer for all models (figure only, no numbers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharing a script across related languages increases within-model cross-lingual representation similarity of parallel sentences in deeper layers.

record.problems: The CKA results are presented in a figure without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not test model-scale effects and notes that experiments across many model scales were not possible.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream task scores and tokenizer statistics were left out because they do not measure representation alignment.

untested.parts: No cross-model comparison on identical inputs and no scale sweep. ALBERT 11M vs RemBERT 192M differ in data and languages, and no cross-model alignment is computed.
No comparison across pretraining seeds. The nine seeds are fine-tuning seeds used only for downstream scores.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
Only CKA is used. No metric, setting or out-of-distribution comparison.
No test of plateau or of the causes of cross-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: No relation category fits exactly: the paper neither tests nor cites the convergence originals. It discusses a related construct (cross-lingual similarity within one model), so it is classed as discusses/T6. The reader's 'tests/T3' is wrong, since no version is tested. The CKA results are figure-only with no numbers. The Appendix E per-language-pair figures add nothing bearing on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep or test of whether increasing size or capability raises alignment; CKA compares language representations within each model, not independently trained models' representations of the same inputs across architectures, objectives, and data.
No vision-language models or image-caption pairs.
No comparison of training seeds for shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No comparison of similarity metrics, metric settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.
No test of whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete, or whether shared data or objectives explain alignment.
